claims.claim: Jupiter is the biggest planet in the solar system. (Opening hook: a viewer who swipes here leaves with this fact only.)
claims.note: Jupiter has the largest diameter (142,984 km) and mass (1898e24 kg) of the eight planets. The first sentence is true on its own, so A4 passes for the opening.

claims.claim: Two and a half times the mass of every other planet combined.
claims.note: Jupiter 1898.13e24 kg. Mercury+Venus+Earth+Mars+Saturn+Uranus+Neptune = 0.330+4.87+5.97+0.642+568+86.8+102 = 768.6e24 kg. Ratio 2.47, so 'two and a half' is fair rounding.

claims.claim: JUPITER / 2.5× every other planet
claims.note: Without 'combined' and 'mass' the label says Jupiter is 2.5 times EACH other planet. That is false: Jupiter is 3.3x Saturn's mass and about 2.8x Saturn's diameter. Change the label to '2.5× the mass of all other planets combined' (or '2.5× all the other planets combined, by mass').

claims.claim: But hold Jupiter up next to the Sun, and it disappears.
claims.note: Low severity, but it is hyperbole a pedant can break: Jupiter's mean radius (69,911 km) is about 1/10 of the Sun's (695,700 km). Next to the Sun it is a small disc, clearly visible, not gone. Suggest 'and it looks tiny' or 'it is a tenth of the Sun's width'.

claims.claim: You could pour a thousand Jupiters into the Sun and still have room left over.
claims.note: Contradicted by the cited figures. Sun volume 1,412,000e12 km^3 divided by Jupiter volume 143,128e10 km^3 gives 986.5. A thousand Jupiters (1.431e18 km^3) are about 1.4% MORE than the Sun's volume, so they overflow and leave no room. Solid spheres would pack even worse (about 600 to 700). SOURCES entry 2 reports ~986 but still concludes 'room left over'. Change to 'You could pour nearly a thousand Jupiters into the Sun' or 'It would take about a thousand Jupiters to fill the Sun', and correct SOURCES entry 2.

claims.claim: ≈ 1,000 JUPITERS / and room left over
claims.note: '≈ 1,000' is fine for 986.5, but 'and room left over' is false (see claim 5). Change the sub-line to 'to fill it', or drop it.

claims.claim: And here is the part that gets people. Our Sun is not a big star. It is not even average.
claims.source_checked: https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2021/06/aa40985-21/T3.html (Reylé et al. 2021, A&A 650, A201, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985, Table 3)
claims.note: Fails A3/A4. In plain English 'not even average' means BELOW average, and the line is framed as the surprise reveal. A viewer who swipes here leaves believing the Sun is a small, below-average star. The census says the opposite: within 10 pc there are A 4, F 8, G 18, K 38, M 249 and white dwarfs 20, so only about 5 to 9% of stars are G2 or earlier. The script's own next line and ending say the Sun is above average, so it contradicts itself. Change to something like 'Our Sun is not an average star. It is bigger than almost all of them.'

claims.claim: It is heavier and brighter than about ninety percent of the stars in our galaxy.
claims.note: The direction is right but the figure is soft and the SOURCES entry cites no A2 source ('figures of 85-95% are quoted'). Reylé 2021 Table 3 (10 pc, Sun excluded): A 4, F 8, G 18, K 38, M 249, white dwarfs 20, plus 41 untyped (the paper says 36 of them are possible M dwarfs). Even if every G star counted as at least as massive as the Sun (they do not: Tau Ceti and others are late G), the Sun outweighs about 91% of typed stars. The realistic count (A, F and only the G0 to G2 or evolved G stars) is about 95%. Change to 'more than ninety percent', which holds under every reading. Re-cite SOURCES entry 3 to Reylé et al. 2021 with these counts. Also note that this is the solar-neighbourhood census used as the standard proxy for the galaxy; the paper does not itself say 'galaxy'.

claims.claim: because most stars are red dwarfs: small, dim, and everywhere.
claims.note: 249 M stars out of 337 typed stars is 74%. The paper's own figures are 58.9 ± 5.8% of all typed objects including brown dwarfs, and about 61% of stars plus brown dwarfs. Every reading is a majority. The 'because' is fair as the main reason, though K dwarfs (38) and white dwarfs (20) are also needed to get past 90%. SOURCES entry 4 says 'uncontested' with no citation (A1); add Reylé 2021.

claims.claim: THE SUN / bigger than 9 stars in 10
claims.note: True under the census even in the worst case: about 91% of stars are smaller, and about 95% realistically. All K, M and white-dwarf stars are smaller in radius than the Sun. This only passes once SOURCES entry 3 cites Reylé 2021 (A1/A6). If the spoken line moves to 'more than ninety percent', this label still matches.

claims.claim: Grid of 100 dots: 10 bright (stars at least as big as the Sun), 90 dim, Proxima Centauri one of the dim ones; label 'THE SUN / one of the ten'
claims.where: on-screen: star grid / THE SUN one of the ten
claims.note: The grid makes a quantity claim: 10% of stars are at least as big as the Sun. The census gives about 5% (A 4 + F 8 + roughly a third of the 18 G stars + the Sun, out of about 375 stars). Even the impossible upper bound, counting every G star, is 31/338, about 9%. So the grid overstates the number of Sun-sized stars by up to 2x. Draw 5 bright dots of 100 and change the label to 'one of the five' (or 'one of the few'), or add on-screen text saying it is illustrative and not to scale (A6). Proxima as a dim dot is correct (M5.5 V).

claims.claim: So look at the nearest star to our own. Proxima Centauri,
claims.source_checked: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature19106 (Anglada-Escudé et al. 2016, Nature 536, 437; abstract read via search excerpt of the paper page)
claims.note: The abstract says Proxima Centauri, at 1.295 pc, 'is the Sun's closest stellar neighbour'. The SOURCES entry cites no A2 source ('uncontested'); add this or the Reylé 2021 catalogue.

claims.claim: just over four light years away.
claims.note: sy_dist = 1.30119 ± 0.00034 pc, which is 4.244 ly. The SOURCES entry gives 4.2465 ly, the Gaia DR3 value, which I could not open (ESA archive and CDS unreachable). Either way the wording 'just over four light years' holds. SOURCES should name the catalogue (Gaia DR3, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202243940) instead of 'uncontested'.

claims.claim: The closest star there is,
claims.note: False as worded: the closest star there is, to us, is the Sun (a G2 V star, 1 AU away). This is the exact pedant comment the channel promises to survive. Change to 'The closest star to the Sun' or 'Our nearest neighbour'.

claims.claim: and you have never seen it. It is too faint for your eyes,
claims.source_checked: https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.02001 (Howard et al. 2018, ApJL 860, L30, doi:10.3847/2041-8213/aacaf3) ; NASA Exoplanet Archive (sy_vmag 11.01, TICv8)
claims.note: Normally true: V ≈ 11.0, far below the naked-eye limit. But Howard et al. 2018 report 'the first naked-eye-brightness superflare detected from Proxima Centauri' (March 2016, a 68x brightening) and predict at least five superflares a year. An absolute 'too faint for your eyes' is breakable. Change to 'It is almost always too faint for your eyes' (or 'normally'). The naked-eye limit of ~6 in SOURCES entry 6 also has no A2 citation; Howard 2018 supports it implicitly, since ~11 mag brightened 68x reaches naked-eye brightness.

claims.claim: and too faint for most binoculars.
claims.source_checked: https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1990PASP..102..212S/abstract (Schaefer 1990, Telescopic Limiting Magnitudes; abstract only via search, no binocular figure); ADS full text not reachable from this session
claims.note: The SOURCES entry gives '10x50 reach about 9.5-10.5' with no citation (A1/A2). I could not open a standard reference that gives a binocular limiting magnitude, so the claim cannot be confirmed. Add a citable source for binocular limiting magnitude, e.g. a figure computed from Schaefer 1990 PASP 102, 212 for 50 mm and 7x/10x, or cut 'and too faint for most binoculars'.

claims.claim: You need a telescope to find the star next door.
claims.source_checked: script SOURCES entry 6 (internal consistency); Schaefer 1990 abstract as above
claims.note: It overstates its own SOURCES entry, which says large 15x70 binoculars under a dark sky can reach ~11, so a telescope is not strictly needed. 'Too faint for MOST binoculars' and 'you NEED a telescope' cannot both be true. Change to 'You need a telescope, or big binoculars and a dark sky' or 'A small telescope will show it', and source the limiting magnitude (see claim 16).

claims.claim: PROXIMA CENTAURI / 0.15× the Sun's radius
claims.source_checked: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1611.03495 (Kervella et al. 2017, A&A 598, L7, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201629930) ; NASA Exoplanet Archive (st_rad, Suárez Mascareño et al. 2025, 2025A&A...700A..11M)
claims.note: There is no SOURCES entry for this figure (A1/A6). Sources disagree (A3): Kervella 2017 adopts 0.1542 ± 0.0045 R_sun (from the Mann et al. 2015 relation); the NASA Exoplanet Archive adopts 0.141 ± 0.021 R_sun (Suárez Mascareño 2025). Add a SOURCES entry recording both. Either show '≈ 1/7 the Sun's radius' (0.143, inside both ranges) or keep '≈ 0.15×' and say why that value was chosen.

claims.claim: That is what most of the galaxy looks like.
claims.source_checked: https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2021/06/aa40985-21/aa40985-21.html (Reylé et al. 2021) ; NASA Exoplanet Archive (st_spectype M5.5 V)
claims.note: Proxima is M5.5 V. M dwarfs are 74% of typed stars within 10 pc, and 'more than half of the M dwarfs (57.0 ± 7.3%) have spectral types M3.0 V to M5.0 V'. So a mid-M dwarf is the typical star. As with claim 8, the step from the local census to 'the galaxy' should be stated in SOURCES as the standard proxy.

claims.claim: The Sun only looks ordinary because we have never stood next to anything else.
claims.source_checked: none cited in SOURCES (entry 7 covers only the previous line)
claims.note: An unsourced causal claim (A1), and as reasoning it is doubtful: we have never stood next to the Sun either. The checkable reason the Sun seems ordinary is a selection effect: nearly all the stars visible to the naked eye are more luminous than the Sun. Either source that (e.g. from the Bright Star Catalogue or the 10 pc census) and reword, or cut the line.
